footnotes.text: Or 'offerings' for 'gifts'; the Greek term can carry a cultic sense in this context.
The phrase is compressed in Greek: literally, 'for the Lord into/in Jerusalem.' The sense is resources designated for the Lord at Jerusalem.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive denotes carrying something away/to a destination. In English, 'to bring' best fits the movement of gifts toward Jerusalem and reads naturally without losing the directional sense.

'Gifts' is the broad, transparent sense and avoids prematurely narrowing the term to a technical sacrificial offering, though cultic overtones are present from the context and recipient ('for the Lord').

κύριος is rendered by the doctrinal default 'Lord.' The dative here can be represented in English as 'for the Lord' because the gifts are intended for his service/worship at Jerusalem; this also matches the later repeated phrase in the verse.

The verb εὔχομαι in the middle can mean to vow, especially with an object like gifts. 'Have vowed' captures the cultic and promissory force better than the broader 'promised' or the misleading 'prayed.'
The plain lexical sense is 'friends.' While the referent may be court associates or supporters, the Greek does not require a more technical rendering.
This straightforwardly denotes precious metals collectively. 'All the gold and silver' is idiomatic and preserves the comprehensiveness of πᾶν.
The relative with ἐὰν and subjunctive expresses indefiniteness/contingency. 'That may be found' preserves that open-ended sense in smooth English.
χώρα commonly means land/region/country. 'Land of Babylonia' is geographically broad and fits the Greek better than the more administrative 'province.'
The preposition εἰς normally marks motion toward. The first occurrence clearly indicates destination, so 'to Jerusalem' is retained there.

translation.text: Rise up and carry it through[a], for the matter is yours, and we are with you; be strong and act.

footnotes.text: The Greek phrase 'to act strongly' is terse and may also be understood as 'be strong' or, in light of the Hebrew parallel (Ezra 10:4), 'be strong and do it.'

lexical_decisions.rationale: Aorist participle of ἀνίστημι used imperativally in exhortation. 'Rise up' preserves the vivid call to action better than the flatter 'get up.'
Imperative of ἐπιτελέω, meaning to complete or bring to fulfillment. 'Carry it through' gives natural modern English while retaining the sense of decisive completion.

alternatives: for the business belongs to you
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally 'for the matter is toward you,' an idiom indicating responsibility or concern. 'The matter is yours' best captures assigned responsibility in concise English.
Straightforward expression of solidarity; no need to over-interpret.

The phrase is somewhat compressed and awkward in Greek. It most naturally conveys acting with strength/supporting vigorous action. 'To act strongly' preserves the verbal force without importing an explicit object not present in the Greek. The Hebrew parallel in Ezra 10:4 supports an exhortation to strength ('be strong and do it'), which informs but does not override the Greek wording.
